lessons.title: Why Brick and Masonry Tanks Win in African Markets
lessons.body: Let me start with the money. In Kenya, a 10,000-litre plastic tank from Elgon or Kentank retails between KES 85,000 and KES 130,000 depending on wall thickness and delivery distance. A ferrocement tank of the same volume built on site costs roughly KES 45,000 to KES 65,000 in materials if you do the labour yourself. A well-built burnt brick masonry tank lands between KES 38,000 and KES 55,000. That gap is your business case. If you are a contractor in Nakuru, Kisumu, or Thika quoting a school, church, or apartment block for water storage, the client will ask why they should pay plastic prices when bricks are on site. Your answer is cost per litre, thermal performance, and repairability. Brick tanks keep water cooler in the hot months because the mass of the masonry resists temperature swings. When a plastic tank cracks from UV degradation after five years, it is scrap. When a brick tank develops a hairline crack, you patch it with mortar and it keeps serving. That is the pitch. Now the numbers in other markets. In Nigeria, a 10,000-litre GP tank or Sintex tank in Lagos runs NGN 650,000 to NGN 900,000. A masonry tank built with 9-inch sandcrete blocks and rendered inside with waterproof mortar costs NGN 280,000 to NGN 420,000 in materials. In Ghana, a 10,000-litre tank from a Tema supplier is GHS 4,500 to GHS 6,500. A burnt brick or block tank in Kumasi costs GHS 2,800 to GHS 4,000. In South Africa, where plastic rotomoulded tanks are cheap and well distributed, the masonry advantage is narrower, but on farms in Limpopo and the Eastern Cape, a 20,000-litre brick reservoir still beats a JoJo tank on price per litre when you are building three or more. The business model is not just construction. It is maintenance contracts. A brick tank needs inspection every six months, re-plastering every three to five years, and cleaning annually. That is recurring revenue. A plastic tank is a one-time sale. If you are building a water business, you want assets that keep you in the client relationship. Materials matter. In Kenya, machine-cut stone from Ndarugu or Juja is excellent for tank walls because it is dense and takes mortar well. In Nigeria, 9-inch sandcrete blocks are the default, but you must cure them properly or they crumble. In Ghana, burnt clay bricks from Aburi or Kwahu are strong and locally available. In South Africa, cement bricks and stock bricks are common. Whatever you use, the tank is only as good as the mortar and the waterproofing. A brick tank that leaks is a liability, not an asset. Safety first. Masonry tanks are heavy. A 10,000-litre tank holds 10 tonnes of water. The foundation must be designed for that load plus the weight of the walls. On black cotton soil, which is common in parts of Kenya and Nigeria, you must excavate to firm ground and pour a reinforced raft. Do not build on a slope without a retaining design. Do not build near a septic tank or soak pit. Do not build where vehicles can hit the wall. And always provide a lockable cover. Children drown in open tanks every year. Your reputation as a builder depends on the tank not falling over and not drowning anyone. Let me give you a real cost breakdown for a 10,000-litre burnt brick tank in Kenya, built in 2024. Excavation and foundation: KES 12,000. Cement, 30 bags at KES 750: KES 22,500. Sand, 3 tonnes at KES 2,500: KES 7,500. Ballast, 2 tonnes at KES 2,800: KES 5,600. Burnt bricks, 1,200 at KES 25: KES 30,000. Waterproofing additive, 5 litres: KES 4,500. Reinforcement mesh for the raft and ring beam: KES 8,000. Labour, if you hire two masons for 10 days at KES 1,200 per day: KES 24,000. Total: roughly KES 114,100 if you pay labour. If you do it yourself with one helper, you cut that to about KES 90,000. The plastic tank is KES 85,000 to KES 130,000 delivered. So the brick tank is competitive, and it lasts longer. That is the lesson. Brick and masonry tanks are not primitive. They are appropriate technology for African conditions, and they are a business opportunity for contractors who understand cost, durability, and maintenance. In the next four lessons, we will get into design, materials, construction, and waterproofing. For now, remember this: the client does not buy bricks. The client buys water security. Your job is to deliver it at a price that beats plastic and ferrocement, and at a quality that keeps your phone ringing.

lessons.title: Design and Sizing of Brick and Masonry Tanks
lessons.body: Before you lay the first brick, you must design the tank. This is where most African masonry tanks fail. A mason who builds a tank by eye will build a tank that cracks. Water is heavy. A 10,000-litre tank exerts 10 tonnes of pressure on the base and significant lateral pressure on the walls. If the walls are too thin or the foundation is too small, the tank will bulge, crack, and leak. Design is not optional. It is the difference between a 20-year asset and a 2-year liability. Start with volume. One cubic metre equals 1,000 litres. A tank that is 2 metres long, 2 metres wide, and 2.5 metres deep holds 10,000 litres. But you must allow freeboard, which is the space between the water line and the top of the wall. Freeboard should be at least 150 millimetres, preferably 300 millimetres, so that when the tank is full, water does not spill over the sides. So if you want 10,000 litres of usable storage, your internal dimensions might be 2 metres by 2 metres by 2.8 metres deep, with the water line at 2.5 metres. Now wall thickness. For a tank up to 1.5 metres deep, a 230-millimetre wall, which is one brick length or one 9-inch block, is adequate if it is reinforced with ring beams and vertical bars. For tanks 1.5 to 2.5 metres deep, you need a 230-millimetre wall with vertical reinforcement at 400-millimetre centres and horizontal ring beams at the top, middle, and bottom. For tanks deeper than 2.5 metres, you should use a 350-millimetre wall or a 230-millimetre wall with additional buttresses. In Nigeria, a common mistake is to build a 2.5-metre-deep tank with a single 9-inch block wall and no reinforcement. That tank will crack within a year. The lateral pressure of water at 2.5 metres depth is about 25 kilonewtons per square metre, which is significant. You need steel. Reinforcement does not have to be expensive. In Kenya, 10-millimetre bars cost about KES 1,200 for a 12-metre length. For a 10,000-litre tank, you might need 12 to 15 bars, which is KES 15,000 to KES 18,000. That is cheap insurance. In Ghana, 10-millimetre bars are about GHS 90 per length. In Nigeria, they are about NGN 8,000 to NGN 12,000 depending on the market. In South Africa, 10-millimetre rebar is about ZAR 120 per 6-metre length. The foundation is critical. The tank plus water plus walls can weigh 15 to 20 tonnes. The soil must be able to carry that load. If you are on firm clay or murram, a 150-millimetre reinforced raft extending 300 millimetres beyond the tank walls is sufficient. If you are on black cotton soil, you must excavate to 1 metre or more and backfill with compacted murram or hardcore, then pour a 200-millimetre raft with two layers of mesh. If you are on sandy soil, you may need a wider raft or a ring foundation. Always test the soil. Dig a test pit, fill it with water, and see how fast it drains. If it drains within an hour, you have sandy soil and need a wider foundation. If it holds water for a day, you have clay and need to manage expansion. If it drains slowly but steadily, you have loam, which is usually good. Now the shape. Circular tanks are stronger than rectangular tanks because the hoop tension is distributed evenly. But circular brick tanks are harder to build because you need to cut bricks at angles. Rectangular tanks are easier to build and easier to roof. For most African applications, a rectangular tank with rounded internal corners is the best compromise. The rounded corners reduce stress concentration. You can form them with mortar and mesh. Square tanks are the weakest because the corners concentrate stress. If you must build square, use thicker walls and more reinforcement. The roof or cover is part of the design. A tank without a cover will grow algae, breed mosquitoes, and collect debris. In Kenya, a simple reinforced concrete slab cover with a 600-millimetre by 600-millimetre access hatch costs about KES 15,000 in materials. In Nigeria, a timber cover with zinc sheeting is cheaper but less durable. In Ghana, a concrete cover is preferred. The cover must be strong enough to walk on, because someone will walk on it. It must also be lockable. Now the inlet and outlet. The inlet should be at the top, with a mosquito screen. The outlet should be 100 millimetres above the floor to avoid sucking sediment, or you can have a sump below the floor for sediment collection. The overflow should be at the top, sized to handle the maximum inflow. A 50-millimetre overflow is enough for a 10,000-litre tank fed by a 1-inch pipe. The drain should be at the lowest point, with a gate valve. In Kenya, a 1-inch gate valve costs about KES 1,500. In Nigeria, it is about NGN 8,000. Do not use plastic ball valves on a tank drain; they break. Use brass or metal gate valves. Finally, consider the water source. If you are harvesting rainwater from a roof, you need a first-flush diverter to keep dirt out. In Kenya, a simple first-flush diverter made from a 100-millimetre PVC pipe and a float valve costs about KES 3,000. In Ghana, you can make one from a bucket and a ball valve for GHS 150. If you are filling from a borehole or mains, you need a float valve to shut off the supply when the tank is full. A good float valve costs KES 2,500 in Kenya, NGN 15,000 in Nigeria, GHS 200 in Ghana, and ZAR 350 in South Africa. Design is not about drawing pretty plans. It is about making sure the tank does not fail. A tank that fails costs you more than the profit you made. It costs you your reputation. So take the time to size the tank, specify the reinforcement, design the foundation, and plan the plumbing. Your client will thank you, and your business will grow.

lessons.title: Materials and Mortar for Brick and Masonry Tanks
lessons.body: The materials you choose determine whether your tank lasts 20 years or 2 years. In Africa, we have excellent local materials, but we also have a lot of substandard materials. Your job as a builder is to know the difference and to refuse to use junk. Let me go through the materials one by one. Bricks. Burnt clay bricks are the best for water tanks because they are dense, strong, and dimensionally stable. In Kenya, bricks from Ndarugu, Juja, and Thika are good. In Ghana, bricks from Aburi and Kwahu are good. In Nigeria, burnt bricks are less common, but you can find them in Abeokuta and Ibadan. In South Africa, clay bricks from Vereeniging and Clayville are good. A good burnt brick rings when you strike it and does not crumble when you scratch it. If a brick absorbs water like a sponge, it is underfired and will fail in a water tank. Test bricks by soaking them in water for 24 hours. A good brick will absorb less than 15 percent of its weight. A bad brick will absorb 25 percent or more. If you are using sandcrete blocks, which are common in Nigeria and Ghana, make sure they are cured for at least 21 days. Many block makers sell blocks after 3 days. Those blocks are weak and will crack. You can also make your own blocks on site. A 9-inch block mix is 1 part cement to 6 parts sand. For a water tank, use 1 part cement to 5 parts sand for extra strength. In Kenya, a 9-inch block costs about KES 60 to KES 80. In Nigeria, it is NGN 250 to NGN 400. In Ghana, it is GHS 4 to GHS 6. In South Africa, a cement brick is ZAR 6 to ZAR 10. Cement. Use fresh cement. Cement that has lumps is old and weak. In Kenya, Simba, Bamburi, and Mombasa Cement are reliable. In Nigeria, Dangote and BUA are reliable. In Ghana, Ghacem and Diamond are reliable. In South Africa, PPC and AfriSam are reliable. For tank construction, use 32.5 or 42.5 grade cement. Do not use 32.5 for the raft if you can avoid it; use 42.5 for the raft and 32.5 for the walls. A bag of cement in Kenya is KES 700 to KES 800. In Nigeria, it is NGN 7,000 to NGN 9,000. In Ghana, it is GHS 60 to GHS 80. In South Africa, it is ZAR 90 to ZAR 120. Sand. Use clean river sand or pit sand. Do not use sand with clay or silt. Test it by putting a handful in a bottle of water and shaking it. If the water is muddy after an hour, the sand has too much clay. Good sand should be sharp and gritty. In Kenya, river sand from Athi River is good. In Nigeria, sharp sand from Lagos and Ogun is good. In Ghana, sand from the Volta River is good. In South Africa, river sand from the Vaal is good. A tonne of sand in Kenya is KES 2,000 to KES 3,000. In Nigeria, it is NGN 15,000 to NGN 25,000 per trip. In Ghana, it is GHS 300 to GHS 500 per trip. In South Africa, it is ZAR 400 to ZAR 600 per tonne. Ballast or aggregate. For the raft, use 20-millimetre crushed stone or river ballast. In Kenya, ballast is KES 2,500 to KES 3,500 per tonne. In Nigeria, it is NGN 20,000 to NGN 30,000 per trip. In Ghana, it is GHS 400 to GHS 600 per trip. In South Africa, it is ZAR 500 to ZAR 700 per tonne. Water. Use clean water. Do not use water from a muddy river or a salty borehole. Salt water will corrode reinforcement and weaken mortar. If you must use borehole water, test it for salinity. In coastal areas of Kenya, Nigeria, and Ghana, salinity is a real problem. Reinforcement. Use 10-millimetre or 12-millimetre deformed bars for vertical and horizontal reinforcement. In Kenya, 10-millimetre bars are KES 1,200 per 12-metre length. In Nigeria, they are NGN 8,000 to NGN 12,000 per 12-metre length. In Ghana, they are GHS 90 to GHS 120 per 12-metre length. In South Africa, they are ZAR 120 to ZAR 150 per 6-metre length. Use binding wire to tie the bars. In Kenya, a roll of binding wire is KES 1,500. In Nigeria, it is NGN 10,000. In Ghana, it is GHS 100. In South Africa, it is ZAR 150. Waterproofing. This is the most important material after cement. You can use integral waterproofing powder or liquid, or you can use a cement-based waterproof coating. In Kenya, a 5-litre bottle of integral waterproofing liquid costs KES 4,000 to KES 6,000. In Nigeria, it is NGN 20,000 to NGN 30,000. In Ghana, it is GHS 250 to GHS 400. In South Africa, it is ZAR 300 to ZAR 500. You can also use bitumen-based coatings, but they are not recommended for potable water. For potable water, use cement-based coatings or integral waterproofing that is certified for drinking water. Mortar mix. For brick and block walls, use 1 part cement to 4 parts sand for the bed joints, and 1 part cement to 3 parts sand for the internal render. Add waterproofing to the render mix. For the raft, use 1 part cement to 2 parts sand to 4 parts ballast. For the ring beams, use 1 part cement to 2 parts sand to 3 parts ballast. Do not use too much water in the mix. A stiff mix is stronger than a wet mix. If the mortar runs off the trowel, it is too wet. Finally, consider the cost of transport. In many parts of Africa, transport costs more than the materials. In Kenya, a lorry of sand from Athi River to Nakuru costs KES 15,000. In Nigeria, a lorry of sand from Ogun to Lagos costs NGN 50,000. In Ghana, a trip from the Volta River to Kumasi costs GHS 800. In South Africa, a delivery from the Vaal to Limpopo costs ZAR 2,000. Always source materials as close to the site as possible. If you are building in a rural area, you may need to make your own blocks or bricks on site. That is fine. It reduces cost and creates local employment. But you must cure them properly. A block that is not cured is a block that will fail. So there you have it. Materials matter. Do not compromise. Your tank is only as good as the materials you put into it. Use good bricks, good cement, clean sand, strong reinforcement, and proper waterproofing. Your client will get a tank that lasts, and you will get a reputation that brings more work.

lessons.title: Step-by-Step Construction of a Brick Water Tank
lessons.body: Now we get to the actual building. This is where theory meets practice. I will walk you through the construction of a 10,000-litre rectangular burnt brick tank, but the same steps apply to block tanks and larger or smaller tanks. The sequence is: setting out, excavation, foundation, walls, ring beams, render, waterproofing, cover, plumbing, and testing. Do not skip steps. Each step depends on the one before it. Step 1: Setting out. Clear the site. Mark the footprint of the tank using pegs and string. Add 300 millimetres on all sides for the foundation. Check the diagonals to make sure the corners are square. If the diagonals are not equal, your tank will be skewed. Use a spirit level to check that the ground is level. If it is not, you will need to cut and fill. Step 2: Excavation. Excavate to the depth required by your design. For a 10,000-litre tank on firm soil, excavate 300 millimetres for the raft. On black cotton soil, excavate 1 metre and backfill with murram. Compact the bottom with a hand rammer or a plate compactor. If you do not compact, the foundation will settle and crack. Step 3: Foundation. Pour a 100-millimetre blinding layer of lean concrete, 1 part cement to 8 parts sand to 16 parts ballast. Then place the reinforcement mesh. For a 10,000-litre tank, use 10-millimetre bars at 200-millimetre centres both ways, with 50 millimetres of cover. Pour the raft, 150 millimetres thick, using 1 part cement to 2 parts sand to 4 parts ballast. Vibrate or rod the concrete to remove air pockets. Level the top with a straight edge. Cure the raft for at least 7 days by covering it with wet sacks or plastic. Do not walk on it for 3 days. Step 4: Walls. Mark the internal dimensions on the raft. Start laying bricks at the corners. Use a string line to keep the courses straight. Check with a spirit level every course. The mortar joint should be 10 to 12 millimetres thick. Do not make the joints too thick; thick joints are weak. As you build, place vertical reinforcement bars in the mortar joints at 400-millimetre centres. These bars should be tied to the raft reinforcement. Build the walls in lifts of 1 metre per day. If you build too fast, the mortar will not set and the wall will bulge. After each lift, fill the hollows in the blocks with mortar or concrete. For burnt bricks, the wall is solid, so you do not need to fill. Step 5: Ring beams. At the top of the wall, and at mid-height if the tank is deeper than 1.5 metres, build a reinforced concrete ring beam. The ring beam should be 150 millimetres by 150 millimetres, with four 10-millimetre bars and 6-millimetre stirrups at 200-millimetre centres. The ring beam ties the walls together and resists the lateral pressure of the water. Without a ring beam, the walls will crack. Step 6: Internal render. After the walls have cured for at least 14 days, render the inside with a 1:3 cement-sand mortar, 20 millimetres thick. Add integral waterproofing to the render mix. Apply the render in two coats: a scratch coat and a finish coat. The scratch coat should be 10 millimetres thick and scored to provide a key for the finish coat. The finish coat should be 10 millimetres thick and troweled smooth. Round the internal corners with a fillet of mortar. Do not leave sharp corners; they crack. Step 7: Waterproofing. After the render has cured for 7 days, apply a cement-based waterproof coating. Mix the powder with water according to the manufacturer's instructions. Apply two coats with a brush, allowing 4 hours between coats. The coating should be 1 to 2 millimetres thick. Do not use bitumen or tar; they are not safe for drinking water. If you are using integral waterproofing in the render, you may not need an additional coating, but I recommend it for extra safety. Step 8: External render. Render the outside with a 1:4 cement-sand mortar, 15 millimetres thick. This protects the bricks from rain and gives a finished look. You can add a color pigment if you want. Step 9: Cover. Cast a reinforced concrete cover slab, 100 millimetres thick, with 8-millimetre bars at 150-millimetre centres both ways. Leave a 600-millimetre by 600-millimetre access hatch with a lockable lid. The cover must be strong enough to walk on. Alternatively, you can use treated timber joists and zinc sheeting, but concrete is better. Step 10: Plumbing. Install the inlet, outlet, overflow, and drain. Use PVC pipes. The inlet should have a mosquito screen. The outlet should be 100 millimetres above the floor. The overflow should be at the top, with a screen. The drain should be at the lowest point, with a gate valve. Use solvent cement to join PVC pipes. Do not use rubber couplings inside the tank; they leak. Step 11: Testing. Fill the tank with water slowly. Do not fill it in one day. Fill it to 25 percent, wait 24 hours, and check for leaks. Fill to 50 percent, wait 24 hours, and check. Fill to 75 percent, wait 24 hours, and check. Fill to 100 percent, wait 48 hours, and check. If you see damp patches on the outside, mark them and repair them after draining. A small leak will become a big leak if you ignore it. Step 12: Curing and commissioning. After testing, drain the tank and let it dry for 2 days. Then fill it again and add chlorine at 5 milligrams per litre to disinfect. Wait 24 hours, drain, and fill again. Now the tank is ready for use. Throughout construction, keep safety in mind. Wear gloves when handling cement. Wear goggles when cutting bricks. Do not work at heights without a scaffold. Do not let children play near the excavation. Do not leave the tank open overnight. A brick tank is a valuable asset, but it is also a hazard during construction. Build safely, and you will build well.

lessons.title: Waterproofing, Maintenance, and Business Growth
lessons.body: A brick tank that leaks is a failed tank. Waterproofing is not a single step; it is a system. It starts with the mix design, continues through the render, and ends with the coating. If you get it right, the tank will last for decades. If you get it wrong, you will be back on site within a year, fixing leaks for free. That is not a business; that is a charity. Let me explain the waterproofing system in detail. First, the concrete raft must be dense and well-cured. A porous raft will allow water to seep through the floor. Use a low water-cement ratio, 0.5 or less, and cure for at least 7 days. Add integral waterproofing to the raft mix. Second, the wall mortar must be dense. Use 1:4 cement-sand mortar for the bed joints and 1:3 for the internal render. Add integral waterproofing to the render. Third, the render must be applied in two coats and cured properly. Do not let the render dry too fast. In hot weather, cover it with wet sacks and keep it damp for 7 days. Fourth, apply a cement-based waterproof coating. In Kenya, products like Sika 1, MasterSeal, and Fosroc are reliable. In Nigeria, products like Sika, Bostik, and Ardex are reliable. In Ghana, Sika and Ghacem waterproofing are reliable. In South Africa, Sika, ABE, and a.b.e. are reliable. Apply two coats, and make sure the second coat covers the first completely. Fifth, seal the joints between the walls and the floor, and between the walls and the cover. Use a flexible sealant or a mortar fillet. These joints are where leaks start. Now maintenance. A brick tank needs annual cleaning. Drain the tank, scrub the walls with a stiff brush and a chlorine solution, and rinse. Do not use soap or detergent; they leave residue. Inspect the render for cracks. Small cracks can be filled with a cement slurry. Large cracks need to be cut out and re-rendered. Inspect the cover for cracks and the hatch for a good seal. Inspect the inlet, outlet, overflow, and drain for blockages. Replace the mosquito screens if they are torn. Check the gate valve for leaks. In Kenya, a maintenance visit for a 10,000-litre tank takes half a day and costs the client KES 5,000 to KES 8,000. In Nigeria, it is NGN 30,000 to NGN 50,000. In Ghana, it is GHS 300 to GHS 500. In South Africa, it is ZAR 800 to ZAR 1,500. If you have 50 tanks on a maintenance contract, that is a steady income. Now business growth. Brick and masonry tank construction is a competitive business, but there is plenty of work. Schools, clinics, churches, mosques, apartment blocks, farms, and factories all need water storage. The key is to differentiate yourself. Do not compete on price alone. Compete on quality, warranty, and service. Offer a 5-year warranty on your tanks. That sounds risky, but if you build well, you will not have many claims. A warranty is a marketing tool. It tells the client that you stand behind your work. Offer a maintenance contract. That gives you recurring revenue and keeps you in touch with the client. Offer a referral bonus. If a client refers another client, give them a discount on their next service. That is how you grow. Let me give you a real example. In 2023, a contractor in Nakuru, Kenya, built 12 brick tanks for a school network. Each tank was 10,000 litres. The contract was KES 1.2 million. Materials cost KES 600,000. Labour cost KES 300,000. Profit was KES 300,000. That is a 25 percent margin. The contractor then signed a maintenance contract for KES 60,000 per year for all 12 tanks. That is KES 5,000 per tank per year. Over 5 years, that is another KES 300,000. The contractor used the profit to buy a pickup and hire two more masons. Now he is building 30 tanks a year. That is the power of recurring revenue. In Nigeria, a contractor in Ibadan built 20 tanks for a housing estate. Each tank was 5,000 litres. The contract was NGN 4 million. Materials cost NGN 2 million. Labour cost NGN 1 million. Profit was NGN 1 million. He then trained local youths to build tanks and expanded to Abeokuta and Lagos. In Ghana, a contractor in Kumasi built 15 tanks for a church network. Each tank was 8,000 litres. The contract was GHS 60,000. Materials cost GHS 30,000. Labour cost GHS 15,000. Profit was GHS 15,000. He used the profit to buy a block-making machine and now sells blocks to other builders. In South Africa, a contractor in Polokwane built 10 tanks for a farm. Each tank was 20,000 litres. The contract was ZAR 400,000. Materials cost ZAR 200,000. Labour cost ZAR 100,000. Profit was ZAR 100,000. He now specializes in farm water systems and has a waiting list. The lesson is simple. Brick and masonry tanks are a viable business. They are cheaper than plastic, more durable than ferrocement, and more appropriate than concrete in many African contexts. But you must build them well. You must waterproof them properly. You must maintain them. And you must treat your clients as partners, not as one-time sales. If you do that, you will build a business that lasts as long as your tanks. A final word on safety. Water tanks are dangerous. A full 10,000-litre tank weighs 10 tonnes. If it collapses, it can kill. Always follow the design. Always use the right materials. Always test before you hand over. Always lock the hatch. Always teach the client how to maintain the tank. And always carry insurance. In Kenya, contractor insurance costs about KES 50,000 per year. In Nigeria, it is about NGN 200,000. In Ghana, it is about GHS 2,000. In South Africa, it is about ZAR 5,000. That is a small price for peace of mind. Now go out there and build. Africa needs water storage. You have the skills. You have the materials. You have the market. The only thing left is to start.

quiz.q: Which material is most commonly used for constructing masonry water tanks?
quiz.explanation: Bricks with cement mortar are the traditional materials for masonry water tank construction.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a mortar joint in brick masonry tanks?
options: B) Bonding bricks and sealing gaps
quiz.explanation: Mortar bonds the bricks together and seals gaps to prevent water leakage.

quiz.q: Which type of brick is best suited for water tank construction?
options: B) First class burnt clay bricks
quiz.explanation: First class burnt clay bricks have low water absorption and high strength.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mortar mix for water retaining masonry?
quiz.explanation: A 1:3 cement sand mortar is commonly recommended for water retaining structures.

quiz.q: What is the minimum thickness of a brick wall for a small water tank?
quiz.explanation: A half brick wall of 115 mm is too weak; a 230 mm wall is the minimum for small tanks.

quiz.q: Why is a rich cement mortar used on the inner face of a masonry water tank?
quiz.explanation: A rich mortar layer on the inner face helps make the tank watertight.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of providing a cement plaster on masonry tank walls?
quiz.explanation: Cement plaster provides a smooth, waterproof surface on masonry tank walls.

quiz.q: Which admixture is commonly added to mortar to improve water tightness?
quiz.explanation: Integral waterproofing compounds reduce permeability of mortar.

quiz.q: What is the function of a coping in a masonry water tank?
options: B) To protect the top of walls from damage
quiz.explanation: Coping is a protective cap on top of walls to prevent damage and water entry.

quiz.q: Which foundation type is suitable for a small masonry water tank on firm soil?
quiz.explanation: A strip footing is adequate for small masonry tanks on firm soil.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of cracking in masonry water tanks?
options: B) Differential settlement and thermal movement
quiz.explanation: Differential settlement and thermal movements commonly cause cracks in masonry tanks.

quiz.q: Which test is used to check the water tightness of a masonry tank?
quiz.explanation: The water filling test checks leakage and water tightness of the tank.

quiz.q: What is the recommended curing period for masonry water tank walls?
quiz.explanation: Curing for 7 to 14 days is generally recommended for masonry tank walls.

quiz.q: Why is lime sometimes added to cement mortar in masonry tanks?
quiz.explanation: Lime improves workability and water retention of mortar.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a base slab in a masonry water tank?
options: A) To support walls and resist uplift
quiz.explanation: The base slab supports the walls and resists upward water pressure.

quiz.q: Which joint is used to accommodate movement in large masonry tanks?
quiz.explanation: Expansion joints accommodate thermal and moisture movements in large tanks.

quiz.q: What is the minimum grade of cement recommended for water retaining structures?
quiz.explanation: OPC 43 grade or higher is generally recommended for water retaining structures.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of masonry water tanks?
options: B) Susceptibility to cracks and leakage
quiz.explanation: Masonry tanks are prone to cracks and leakage if not properly constructed.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a rich mortar layer at the base of a masonry tank?
options: B) To provide waterproofing at the base
quiz.explanation: A rich mortar layer at the base helps prevent water seepage from the bottom.

quiz.q: Which type of masonry is preferred for circular water tanks?
quiz.explanation: Reinforced brick masonry is preferred for circular tanks due to hoop tension.

quiz.q: What is the function of hoop reinforcement in circular masonry tanks?
quiz.explanation: Hoop reinforcement resists the tensile forces caused by water pressure in circular tanks.

quiz.q: Which factor is most important in selecting bricks for water tank construction?
quiz.explanation: Low water absorption is critical for bricks used in water retaining structures.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness of cement plaster on the inner face of a masonry tank?
quiz.explanation: A 20 mm thick cement plaster is commonly recommended for the inner face.

quiz.q: Why is a waterproof coating applied on the inner surface of masonry tanks?
quiz.explanation: Waterproof coatings prevent leakage and protect the masonry from water penetration.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of masonry water tanks over concrete tanks?
options: B) Lower cost and easy availability of materials
quiz.explanation: Masonry tanks are generally cheaper and use locally available materials.

quiz.q: Which code provides guidelines for construction of masonry water tanks in India?
quiz.explanation: IS 3370 provides guidelines for concrete and masonry water retaining structures.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a lean concrete base under a masonry tank?
options: A) To provide a level working surface
quiz.explanation: Lean concrete provides a level and clean working surface for masonry construction.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common repair method for leaking masonry tanks?
options: B) Grouting cracks and applying waterproof coating
quiz.explanation: Grouting cracks and applying waterproof coatings are common repair methods.

quiz.q: What is the recommended slope for the bottom of a masonry water tank?
quiz.explanation: A slope of about 1 in 100 is recommended for drainage and cleaning.
